results.title: Bounds for element size in a variable stiffness cohesive finite element model | Scilit
results.content: # Bounds for element size in a variable stiffness cohesive finite element model. + Published by Wiley in International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering. + Vol. 61  (11) , 1894-1920. ##### Abstract. The cohesive finite element method (CFEM) allows explicit modelling of fracture processes. One form of CFEM models integrates cohesive surfaces along all finite element boundaries, facilitating the explicit resolution of arbitrary fracture paths and fracture patterns. This framework also permits explicit account of arbitrary microstructures with multiple length scales, allowing the effects of material heterogeneity, phase morphology, phase size and phase distribution to be quantified. However, use of this form of CFEM with cohesive traction–separation laws with finite initial stiffness imposes two competing requirements on the finite element size. On one hand, an upper bound is needed to ensure that fields within crack‐tip cohesive zones are accurately described. On the other hand, a lower bound is also required to ensure that the discrete model closely approximates the physical problem at hand. Both issues are analysed in this paper within the context of fracture in multi‐phase composite microstructures and a variable stiffness bilinear cohesive model. The resulting criterion for solution convergence is given for meshes with uniform, cross‐triangle elements. A series of calculations is carried out to illustrate the issues discussed and to verify the criterion given. These simulations concern dynamic crack growth in an Al2O3 ceramic and in an Al2O3/TiB2 ceramic composite whose phases are modelled as being hyperelastic in constitutive behaviour. results.title: ANSYS Fluent Basics: Understanding Mesh, Grid Independence & Quality Criteria,Step-by-Step Tutorial
results.content:
AY LINGAYAT
156 subscribers
26 likes
595 views
5 Jan 2025
Introduction to Discretization & Meshing (00:00 - 00:42)

Discretization is the process of breaking down continuous domains into smaller elements (grids) to make problems solvable by computational tools. This is essential for accurate simulation results.
Meshing Methods in ANSYS Fluent (01:24 - 02:37)

For 2D geometries: common methods include quadrilateral, triangular, and hybrid (Tria/Quad).
For 3D geometries: methods like tetrahedral, hexahedral, and sweep mesh are used depending on geometry complexity.
Mesh Refinement and Bias (03:19 - 05:12)

Refining the mesh near walls helps capture better fluid behavior.
Mesh sizing and bias (gradual change of element size) are critical for accuracy, especially in CFD simulations. Growth rate controls how the element sizes increase away from walls.
Mesh Quality and Criteria (05:49 - 07:09)

ANSYS Fluent offers automatic mesh quality checks like orthogonality, aspect ratio, skewness, and Jacobian to evaluate the mesh quality.
These parameters ensure that the mesh does not distort, affecting simulation results.
Types of Meshes: Structured vs. Unstructured (07:47 - 09:42)

Structured meshes (e.g., hexagonal for 3D geometries) offer better convergence and memory efficiency but are suited for simpler geometries.
Unstructured meshes are faster to generate and more flexible but can lead to less efficient results.
Mesh Sizing for 2D Geometries (10:26 - 11:14)

Example of meshing a rectangular geometry into smaller elements, calculating element size along both directions to ensure uniformity.
Smooth Transition in Mesh (11:50 - 12:28)

A smooth transition in mesh size is essential for accurate results, particularly in regions with steep gradients, like near walls. The bias factor helps control this transition in structured meshes.
Quality Criteria in Mesh Evaluation (13:08 - 16:00)

Parameters like orthogonal quality, aspect ratio, skewness, and Jacobian determine mesh quality. Ideal values for these are:
Orthogonal quality: Close to 1.
Aspect ratio: Less than 5.
Skewness: Between 0 and 0.25.
Jacobian: Close to 1.
Grid Independence Test (19:18 - 21:46)

A mesh should be refined until the results stabilize and do not significantly change with further mesh refinement. This is called the "grid independence test," which helps to optimize mesh size for simulation accuracy without unnecessary computational cost.
Hands-on Example & Conclusion (23:23 - 37:54)

The tutorial concludes with a hands-on session, showing how adjusting the element size (e.g., from 20 to 5) impacts simulation results (pressure drop).
The optimal element size is determined when further refinement no longer significantly affects the result, improving simulation accuracy and efficiency.
